Listen to this article Share I have never met Jensen Huang. Yet his departure from Nvidia has left me with an unexpected sense of personal loss. For those of us who advocate the responsible adoption of artificial intelligence, he represented something increasingly valuable: an engineer who could explain the machinery of the future and make its possibilities seem tangible. His fall forces an uncomfortable question upon his admirers. How much of our confidence in a technology have we invested in the character of one man? On November 12, 2026, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately. It was an abrupt end to the leadership of a company he had co-founded 33 years earlier. The board appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive and Harvey C. Jones as chair. A permanent successor will be sought from within and outside the company. The circumstances demand precision. On November 8, Huang publicly acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and colleagues. Separately, the board announced an independent investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. At that stage, it said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised. That statement is neither a completed investigation nor proof of wrongdoing beyond what Huang admitted. Reuters has reported his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, and the suspicions of US authorities about her intelligence connections. Beijing has denied that she is a spy. The two Huangs are unrelated. Espionage allegations must remain allegations unless established by evidence and the appropriate proceedings. His resignation does not, by itself, prove that he knowingly assisted a foreign power. None of those distinctions diminishes the seriousness of the crisis. A chief executive responsible for strategically important technology must exercise judgement that protects the institution as well as himself. But responsible commentary requires us to resist the temptation to turn a personal admission, a corporate investigation and national-security suspicions into a single, settled verdict. Huang’s achievement remains extraordinary. Born in Taiwan in 1963, he spent part of his childhood in Thailand before moving to the United States as a boy. He studied electrical engineering at Oregon State University and later earned a master’s degree at Stanford. Before Nvidia, he worked at AMD and LSI Logic. His ascent was rooted in technical training and semiconductor experience, rather than celebrity. In 1993, he founded Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. The discussions at a Denny’s restaurant have become part of Silicon Valley folklore. Their ambition concerned computer graphics, especially gaming and multimedia. The company that would supply essential machinery for the AI revolution began by pursuing the much more immediate challenge of making images on computer screens more compelling. The important insight was that graphics required enormous numbers of calculations to be performed in parallel. The architecture developed for that purpose could serve other demanding computational tasks. Nvidia’s GPU milestone in 1999, followed by its introduction of CUDA in 2006, helped turn graphics hardware into a platform for scientific computing. CUDA gave programmers a practical route to using that processing power beyond graphics. The significance became unmistakable in 2012, when AlexNet demonstrated the power of deep learning in image recognition using Nvidia GPUs. Huang did not invent neural networks or single-handedly create modern AI. His distinction was to recognise the commercial and scientific importance of a computing approach, sustain investment in it, and build an organisation capable of supplying it at scale. That is a more substantial achievement than the familiar description of a man who sold chips during a gold rush. Nvidia built a platform around its processors. The combination of hardware, software and developer familiarity made it useful to customers and increasingly difficult to replace. Its subsequent rise to the world’s most valuable listed company reflected investors’ belief that it occupied a commanding position in the new computing economy. Huang also became its most effective interpreter. The leather jacket, the stagecraft and the expansive keynotes gave a recognisable human face to an industry of bewildering complexity. He could connect the work of engineers with the ambitions of investors and governments. The advantage was considerable. So was the danger of allowing a corporation’s identity to become inseparable from its founder. As recently as 21 October, he was addressing Nvidia’s GTC conference in Berlin. There he presented an account of AI infrastructure that stretched from energy and computing systems to models and applications, while emphasising the need to secure increasingly autonomous AI agents. This last point matters particularly to me. I took encouragement from the prospect that the industry supplying AI’s computational power was also investing in its control. Yet that hope requires technical accuracy. The announcement concerned Nvidia’s OpenShell Reference Architecture for Safe AI Agents, rather than a single GPU capable of guaranteeing that AI would never go rogue. Nvidia describes a combination of software and hardware that can isolate agents, restrict their permissions and monitor their behaviour. Its Sentry framework runs on BlueField data-processing units, providing monitoring outside the agent’s own execution environment. Such architecture aims to make dangerous actions harder to carry out and easier to detect or stop. These are vendor-described capabilities whose effectiveness must be tested in deployment. Containment is valuable, but it is not a universal solution to AI safety. A system might remain within its technical permissions while producing misleading advice or pursuing a poorly specified objective. Security controls must therefore sit alongside evaluation, human accountability and careful decisions about where autonomy is appropriate. No product announcement should be mistaken for proof that humanity’s long-term risks have been resolved. Nvidia now faces a related challenge in corporate form: demonstrating that its controls and capabilities survive the departure of the individual most closely associated with them. Kress, who joined in 2013, brings deep knowledge of its finances and operations. Jones brings technology-industry experience. Their immediate task should be to preserve execution while making the investigation credible. The public announcement establishes an interim arrangement and a search; it does not identify a permanent heir. The board should resist the pressure to recruit a celebrity merely to reassure the market. Nvidia needs leadership able to retain exceptional engineers, coordinate complex production, sustain customer confidence and navigate geopolitical scrutiny. Investors should seek evidence that those responsibilities are shared across a capable team. Whether a suitable internal candidate or an outsider offers the better answer remains open. The market reaction illustrates the cost of uncertainty. Reuters reported that Nvidia shares fell more than 12 per cent in early trading after the announcement, putting roughly $500 billion of market value at risk at that point. That was an intraday indication, not a verified closing loss. The same report recorded gains in AMD and Broadcom, suggesting that some investors were considering competitive beneficiaries as well as wider industry risk. A lasting global market shock is possible, but it is not inevitable. The transmission channels are straightforward. A fall in a heavily weighted company can depress equity indices and funds that track them. Customers might postpone commitments while they assess continuity. Suppliers could face uncertainty over orders. Tighter export restrictions, if imposed, could change the economics of access to major markets. These are scenarios, not outcomes that can already be attributed to the resignation. The distinction between a loss of confidence and a loss of productive capacity is essential. A leadership crisis does not erase engineering knowledge, installed equipment or customers’ computing requirements. Equally, those assets cannot guarantee flawless execution. Nvidia’s vulnerability lies in the possibility that uncertainty will disrupt decisions, relationships and recruitment long enough for competitors to benefit. The company’s future will turn on questions more useful than speculation about its next charismatic figurehead. Can it deliver its products reliably? Can it demonstrate disciplined oversight of sensitive commercial relationships? Will its customers continue to find its platform worth the price? Can the investigation proceed independently, with findings communicated responsibly? A convincing answer would allow Nvidia to emerge as a more durable institution. A defensive or evasive response would deepen the damage. For Africa, this is also a lesson in technological dependence. Our universities, businesses and public institutions should build AI strategies around skills, suitable infrastructure and clear accountability. Admiration for a foreign technology leader is no substitute for the ability to evaluate suppliers, understand limitations and maintain control over consequential decisions. Sovereignty begins with competence. In my work advocating responsible AI, I have stressed the importance of responsible human oversight. That principle must apply to the people governing technology companies as firmly as it applies to the systems those companies produce. A board cannot treat commercial success as an exemption from scrutiny. Nor should an admirer confuse technical brilliance with infallible personal judgement. I remain grateful for what Huang and his colleagues have contributed to computing. Recognising that contribution does not require excusing his admitted conduct. Concern for his family need not become public intrusion. Respect for the investigation requires withholding conclusions it has not yet reached. A serious assessment of his legacy must be capable of holding all these thoughts together. Do we need another hero? We need talented people with the courage to pursue difficult ideas. We also need institutions that can challenge them, constrain their mistakes and continue their work when they leave. The most reassuring future for AI is one in which responsibility is distributed, independently tested and enforceable. My disappointment is real. So is my hope. It now rests more firmly on a demanding proposition: the institutions entrusted with powerful technology must be strong enough to outlast the people who made us believe in it. About the author: Sonny Iroche is an Oxford-trained artificial intelligence specialist and researcher, having completed the postgraduate AI for Business programme at Saïd Business School, University of Oxford. He is the founder and CEO of GenAI Learning Concepts Ltd. He is a member of Nigeria’s National AI Strategy Committee, UNESCO’s Technical Working Group on the AI Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM) in Nigeria, and the Africa AI Council’s technical working groups on Compute Infrastructure and Skills and Talent under Smart Africa. His work focuses on AI governance, cybersecurity and responsible AI adoption across Africa.
